look_here_first: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — INTRODUCED, usually low cool-season annual. Recognize low soft green flowering tufts, often many small open triangular panicles and folded boat-prow leaf tips. The NEW macro really shows the boat tip, and the NEW four-view photo shows a membrane-like LIGULE at the blade/sheath junction. BOTH details are shared by other Poa: for species confirmation, document an intact rooted tuft (usually no persistent connected rhizomes) and a ripe spikelet of normally bisexual florets. The length of a photographed ligule or green head alone is NOT decisive.

best_field_traits: Cool-season generally annual; persistent biotypes can occur in managed moist turf.
Low flowering tuft with small spreading greenish seedheads; can flower under close mowing.
Young folded blades have prow-like boat-shaped tips; this is a genus clue NOT species-specific.
Ligule membranous around 0.5–3 mm according to Williamson County treatment; no auricles.
Spikelets commonly with bisexual florets; unlike separate-sex Texas bluegrass.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: True same-plant rooted annual tuft and basal tillers, including soil-contact roots (permitted collection only)
Whole low green mature panicle with a centimeter ruler and single spikelet without shaking off florets
Under 10–20×: one intact spikelet with outer glumes and bisexual floret features; lemma hair position and length, measured
One Poa leaf-tip macro and true membranous collar (already supplied via CC licensed references; still collect matched local voucher photo)
crew_field_check: Find the small low flowering tuft and whole open green panicle; compare the existing Harry Rose field photo.
See actual 30× photo of folded boat-PROW tip: same general character in both annual and Texas bluegrass; it is NOT a species shortcut.
See Stefan.lefnaer's source-photo composite: distinguish the actual thin pale membranous LIGULE from surrounding leaf sheath and blade; the white 10-mm photo bar isn't the ligule length.
Follow the same grass into a rooted base: annual P. annua usually forms small tillers and lacks Texas bluegrass-like persistent rhizomes, but some biotypes persist beyond a year.
Inspect ripe spikelets for bisexual florets and measured lemma keels; compare to dioecious Texas bluegrass and possible introduced P. pratensis. If not verified, leave Poa sp.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Contrast native P. arachnifera: perennial connected RHIZOMES and separate male/female flowering individuals; a pistillate female's ripe lemma bases produce dense long cobwebby hair tufts, while P. annua flowers generally bisexual and may have keel/marginal hairs but lacks the massive female web character. Do not guess sex or exact lemma hairs from landscape photos; compare P. pratensis and P. trivialis separately where common lawn grasses overlap.
not_reliable_alone: Boat-shaped grass leaf tip is a genus trait common to both Poa species
One very green or woolly head photographed at a distance, without sex/lemma macro
Ligule without the complete rooted specimen
Treating state native range as a Hays county voucher

visual_comparison.title: Poa annua — annual introduced vs perennial dioecious Texas bluegrass
visual_comparison.subtitle: Existing whole-plant, photographed boat-tip and ligule views plus one newly promoted, physically archived spikelet/palea source photo. Anatomy photographs are source-identified, not local voucher-confirmed.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: BOAT TIP + LIGULE = POA GENUS. P. ANNUA = usually annual and bisexual; P. ARACHNIFERA = perennial rhizomes and separate SEXES with WEBBY female lemma bases.

items.why_it_matters: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.

items.image_role: Flickr/Commons macro photographed in Pasadena at 30×, identified by original photographer as annual bluegrass; illustrates the boat-shaped folded grass leaf TIP, shared by other Poa, not a species diagnostic.
items.caption: The green blade narrows to a blunt folded, keel-like 'prow' tip. The lightened very tip is visible; it may be a worn or dry margin, not a separate auricle. The photographer reported magnification 30×, but supplied no calibrated ruler. This proves the shared Poa leaf tip shape, not annual versus Texas bluegrass.
items.why_it_matters: This is an actual photograph of the genus recognition clue that the former whole-plant picture could not resolve. The tip belongs to Poa annua per source label, but its shape alone never distinguishes P. annua from Texas bluegrass.

items.caption: Four source-photo views show the same kind of grass blade/sheath collar. The bottom view exposes the whitish membranous flap (ligule) exactly where green blade separates from the upper sheath. The genuine 10-mm photo scale sits at bottom; do not confuse the entire pale sheath with the ligule or infer its precise size without local measurement.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches the actual part crews must photograph: a thin membranous ligule at the junction, not a tuft of hairs or a leaf tip. Texas bluegrass also has a membranous ligule; the difference lies primarily in reproductive sex and perennial rhizomes.

Use it to recognize the nested spikelet/floret architecture, then obtain a measured, separated glume/lemma/palea and clearly bisexual floret from a locally verified plant before claiming species-level reproductive confirmation.
